knowledge.statement: For the same lost-entry state, the resolution delivered to `append_notify` differs by tick granularity. Retained run of the three-case probe: mode A (no partition, 2 ms ticks) resolved `ok` with the caller's entry at the returned index; mode B (leader partitioned from both followers, entry accepted only locally, new leader on node 3 decides a different entry at the same index, 2 ms ticks) resolved `superseded` with the origin's decided index still 0 and no decided entries readable; mode C (identical setup, 80 ms ticks) resolved `ok(assigned_idx = 1)` while the origin's decided log at index 1 held the new leader's entry and the caller's entry appeared in no decided log (`entry_equals_submitted` false, origin decided values `22`, origin decided index 1, origin leader pid 3, origin decided index 0 while partitioned).
knowledge.conditions: Three-node cluster, majority quorum, batch_size 1, node 1 the pre-partition leader, message loss modelled as dropped whole messages in an in-process in-memory transport, no node restart (the origin is re-synchronized in-process). The `ok` arm is delivered when the origin's promise change and its decided-index advance both fall inside one tick period; with a tick period near the Prepare/AcceptSync round trip the `superseded` arm is delivered instead. Both arms were observed under this same setup, so neither is a property of the lost-entry state alone.

scope.description: One real in-process cluster shape (three OmniPaxos actors over an in-memory transport, majority quorum, batch_size 1, node 1 forced into the leader role), run three times with different admissions. Mode A (control): no partition, so entry 11 appended through the origin is replicated and decided normally. Modes B and C: node 1's links to both followers are cut in both directions, node 1 - still the leader in the accept phase - takes entry 11 (so it can only be accepted locally and assigned an index), the two followers elect node 3, which decides entry 22 at the same first index, and node 1 is then reconnected so the new leader re-synchronizes it. B and C differ only in the actor tick period (2 ms vs 80 ms), which controls whether a drain_notifiers pass can run between the origin's promise change and its decided-index advance.
assumptions: Message loss/partition is a permitted fault for this protocol; the core tolerates lost messages via its resend path, and the harness drops whole messages inside the transport without adding backpressure.
Each node is a real OmniPaxos instance with MemoryStorage, batch_size 1 and a majority quorum, driven only through the public actor handle; no target logic is modified.

Node 1 carries leader_priority 1 so the pre-partition leader is stable; a higher priority only breaks ties at equal ballot number, and in modes B/C the followers reach a strictly higher ballot number through the election-timeout takeover path, so the priority cannot prevent the new election.

drain_notifiers runs only from the tick branch, so the resolution instant is quantised by tick_period; the gap between the origin's Prepare handling and the AcceptSync that follows it is one round trip (about 2-4 ms here).
excluded: Any claim about entries other than the two submitted values (11 by the origin, 22 by the new leader).
Any claim about transports, runtimes or timings other than the in-process in-memory transport used here.
Durable/crash recovery: the origin is re-synchronized in-process, it is not restarted, so no storage-persistence claim follows from these cases.

experiment.prefix: Per case: build three OmniPaxos instances (pids 1..3, configuration_id 1, nodes [1,2,3], MemoryStorage, batch_size 1, election_tick_timeout 3, node 1 leader_priority 1) and spawn each as an actor through spawn_actor with a tokio-backed AsyncRuntime adapter (tick_period per case, egress_period 1 ms). Wire every node's outgoing_messages() receiver into a task that consults a per-direction block set and, unless the link is blocked, delivers the message with peer.handle_incoming(). Admission: call handles[1].try_become_leader() until all three nodes report current_leader() == (1, true) and still do so after four election timeouts; emit the admission event carrying the mode, the cluster setup, origin 1, submitted_value 11 and the tick period. Mode A: await handles[1].append_notify(TestEntry(11)) and then read the origin's decided suffix. Modes B/C: block (1,2) and (1,3) both ways, spawn handles[1].append_notify(TestEntry(11)) as a task, sleep one tick period, wait until nodes 2 and 3 both report a leader other than 1 with accepted=true, await handles[new_leader].append_notify(TestEntry(22)), then unblock both links and await the origin's future. Emit new_leader_elected, new_leader_append (with the new leader's decided values) and notify_resolution, the last carrying the resolved variant (ok / superseded / timeout / ...), the assigned index, the decided entry at that index and, only when that index was actually observed in the decided log, whether it equals the submitted value.
experiment.responsibility: The decisive inputs are produced by the target itself: the actor assigns the caller's entry an index from its own local accept as leader, records the assignment as (index, ballot) with no entry identity, and drain_notifiers derives the resolution from the local decided index alone, evaluating the Ok arm before the ballot-change arm. The caller supplies only the entry value.

interpretations.rationale: Current account. In this actor layer an `append_notify` assignment is only `(log index, ballot at assignment)` and the success arm of `drain_notifiers` fires on `assigned_idx <= local decided index` alone, evaluated before the ballot-change arm and without ever comparing the caller's entry with what occupies that index. The retained execution shows the consequence end to end on real instances: in mode C the origin was the leader, was partitioned from both followers, and took the caller's entry 11 while partitioned (its decided index stayed 0, so the entry was accepted but never decided); node 3 then won the election among the followers and decided entry 22 at log index 1; after the origin was reconnected and re-synchronized, its `append_notify` for entry 11 resolved `ok` with assigned index 1 while the decided entry at index 1 was 22 and the origin's whole decided log was `22` - entry 11 appears in no decided log. The same call under the control condition (mode A, no partition) resolved `ok` with entry 11 actually at index 1, so the success signal is meaningful in the normal case and false in the lost-entry case; and the identical lost-entry setup with 2 ms ticks (mode B) produced the documented `Superseded` instead, which shows that which signal the caller receives is decided by whether the promise change and the decided-index advance happen to fall in one tick period rather than by the durable outcome of the write. That is the defect: the resolution rule documented for a leader change after acceptance but before decision (Superseded) is bypassed in favour of an unqualified success whenever the two updates share a tick window, and a caller that trusts the success takes its entry to be decided at an index that holds a different value. The claim is scoped to this actor layer, this fault model (whole-message loss, election-timeout takeover) and the batch_size 1 / majority-quorum configuration used here.
counterevidence: The entry-point documentation of `append_notify` only promises to resolve "when the assigned log index is decided" (`handle_append_notify_contract`), and the Superseded doc advises callers to re-read the returned index if they need certainty; under that reading `Ok(idx)` is a claim about the index and not about the caller's value, so a caller that verifies the entry at the returned index is not misled. This weakens the caller-facing consequence but not the schedule-dependence, because the same lost-entry state cannot legitimately yield both `Superseded` and `Ok` if the signal is about state rather than timing.

A new leader must adopt any value a majority-overlapping write quorum already accepted, so an entry that reached a write quorum cannot be replaced; the loss observed here needs the assignment to be local-only, which the retained events support (origin decided index 0 while partitioned, followers' decided values `22` only).

In the retained receipt the controller's three comparisons were evaluated `unknown` (diagnostics: missing `admission_a.origin`/`submitted_value`, no prerequisite events reached), because my admission events lacked the identity fields; the witness above therefore rests on the parsed events of that receipt (indices 1, 5, 9) and on the target sources, not on an evaluated comparison.

The `Superseded` arm itself does not confirm that the caller's entry is decided; it stops waiting. So a caller cannot derive the entry's fate from an error resolution either - the two arms differ in what they claim, not only in optimism.
limitations: In-process in-memory transport, no crash or restart: the origin is re-synchronized from the new leader, not recovered from storage, so nothing here extends to the persistence/fail-recovery path.

One cluster shape and one fault pattern (both directions of the old leader's links dropped, election-timeout takeover, batch_size 1, majority quorum, the second entry appended through the new leader). Other interleavings, batching configurations or flexible quorums are unmeasured.

The schedule dependence is characterised by two tick periods only (2 ms and 80 ms) around a round trip of about 2-4 ms; it bounds neither the frequency of the false success in deployment nor the exact tick/RTT threshold.

The corrected successor execution is submitted in this update; until its receipt exists, the comparison-typed witness for the false success is the parsed event data above, and the comparison chain in the retained receipt remains unevaluated.
